sentences.text: Argentinosaurus is a genus of giant sauropod dinosaur, a name meaning "lizard from Argentina".
The type species of this genus is Argentinosaurus huinculensis.
This animal belonged to Titanosauria, the dominant sauropod group during the Cretaceous period.
A reconstructed dorsal vertebra of the animal measures 159 centimeters in height and 129 centimeters in width.
Estimates suggest the creature measured between 30 and 35 meters long and weighed between 65 and 80 tonnes.
The first bone, identified as a fibula, was discovered in 1987 by a farmer named Guillermo Heredia near Plaza Huincul.
The discovery site was located approximately 8 kilometers east of Plaza Huincul in Neuquén Province, Argentina.
A scientific excavation led by José Bonaparte subsequently took place in 1989.
In 2016, Mark Hallett and Matthew Wedel estimated that Argentinosaurus eggs were likely only 1 liter in volume.
They further estimated that a newly hatched individual was no longer than 1 meter and did not weigh more than 5 kilograms.
It is suggested that Argentinosaurus may have been preyed upon by Mapusaurus, one of the largest known theropods.
The animal is classified under the genus Argentinosaurus, which was described by Bonaparte and Coria in 1993.
Bonaparte and Coria also proposed the family Andesauridae for Argentinosaurus, Andesaurus, and Epachthosaurus.
Argentinosaurus lived during the Albian stage, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.
Fossils were recovered from the Huincul Formation, which was deposited in the Albian stage.
The Huincul Formation consists of fine-to-medium grain yellowish and greenish sandstones, some containing volcanic ash.
Fossilized pollen from the formation indicates a diverse plant environment that included hornworts, ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms.
The fragmentary nature of the remains makes interpreting the animal difficult.
There is disagreement over whether Argentinosaurus was the largest known titanosaur.
In 2019, Paul found Patagotitan to be smaller than Argentinosaurus.
Some authors argue that the hollow dorsal ribs of Argentinosaurus may be due to post-mortem erosion rather than being naturally hollow.
Earlier research suggested the age of the deposits containing Argentinosaurus ranged from the Cenomanian–Turonian to the Early Turonian–Late Santonian.
